questions.question_text: Which statement correctly uses the terms zero, root, and $x$-intercept for $P(x) = (x - 5)(x + 2)$?

options.text: $5$ is a zero of $P(x)$, $x = 5$ is a root of $P(x) = 0$, and $(5, 0)$ is an $x$-intercept of $y = P(x)$
$x = 5$ is a zero of $P(x)$, $5$ is a root of $P(x) = 0$, and $5$ is an $x$-intercept
options.why: Confused the equation form with the number that is a zero of a polynomial.

options.text: $(5, 0)$ is a zero of $P(x)$ and $5$ is an $x$-intercept of $y = P(x)$
options.why: Called the coordinate pair a zero instead of the $x$-intercept.

options.text: $5$ is a root of $P(x)$, $x = 5$ is a zero of $P(x) = 0$, and $(0, 5)$ is an $x$-intercept
options.why: Swapped the definitions of zero and root and reversed the intercept coordinates.

questions.solution_text:
A zero of $P(x)$ is the number $5$.
A root of the equation $P(x) = 0$ is the solution $x = 5$.
An $x$-intercept is the coordinate point $(5, 0)$.

questions.question_text: What is the multiplicity of the zero $x = -3$ in the polynomial $P(x) = (x + 3)^{4}(x - 1)^{2}$?

options.why: Selected the power of the other factor $(x - 1)^{2}$.
Added the powers of all factors together (the degree of $P(x)$).
Treated every zero as a single zero regardless of the exponent.

questions.solution_text:
The factor $(x + 3)$ has exponent $4$.
The zero $x = -3$ has multiplicity $4$.

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y = (x + 2)^{2}(x - 4)$ behave at its $x$-intercepts?

options.text: Touches the axis at $x = -2$ and cuts the axis at $x = 4$
Cuts the axis at $x = -2$ and touches the axis at $x = 4$
options.why: Swapped the behaviours: even multiplicity touches, while odd multiplicity crosses.

options.text: Cuts the axis at both $x = -2$ and $x = 4$
options.why: Assumed the curve crosses the axis at all $x$-intercepts.

options.text: Touches the axis at both $x = -2$ and $x = 4$
options.why: Assumed the curve bounces off the axis at all $x$-intercepts.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = -2$, multiplicity is $2$ (even), so the curve touches (bounces).
At $x = 4$, multiplicity is $1$ (odd), so the curve cuts (crosses).

questions.question_text: Which zero of $P(x) = (x - 6)(x + 1)^{3}(x - 3)^{2}$ produces a horizontal point of inflection on the graph of $y = P(x)$?

options.why: Selected the double root (multiplicity 2), which touches the axis rather than inflecting.
Selected the single root (multiplicity 1), which cuts straight through.
Reversed the sign of the zero from the factor $(x + 1)$.

questions.solution_text:
A horizontal point of inflection occurs where the factor has an odd power $\ge 3$.
The factor $(x + 1)^{3}$ gives a triple zero at $x = -1$.

options.text: A zero of even multiplicity (touches without crossing)
A zero of multiplicity 1 (cuts straight through)
options.why: Claimed the curve crosses the axis at $x = 2$ when it clearly bounces.

options.text: A zero of multiplicity 3 (inflects along the axis)
options.why: Mistook a bouncing parabola shape for a cubic inflection.

options.text: Not a zero of the polynomial
options.why: Claimed an $x$-intercept is not a zero of the polynomial.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = 2$, the curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around without crossing.
This indicates a zero of **even multiplicity** (such as multiplicity $2$).

options.text: The curve flattens with a horizontal tangent as it crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -2$
The curve bounces off the $x$-axis without crossing at $x = -2$
options.why: Described an even multiplicity behaviour instead of an inflection.

options.text: The curve crosses the $x$-axis with a non-zero gradient at $x = -2$
options.why: Described a single zero (multiplicity 1) rather than a triple zero inflection.

options.text: The curve has a $y$-intercept at $x = -2$
options.why: Confused an $x$-intercept with a $y$-intercept.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = -2$, the curve crosses the $x$-axis and momentarily flattens to a horizontal tangent (horizontal inflection).
This confirms multiplicity $3$.

questions.question_text: What is the formula of the monic cubic polynomial that has a double zero at $x = -1$ and a single zero at $x = 4$?

options.why: Copied each zero straight into its bracket instead of subtracting it, so the signs in both linear factors are reversed and the zeroes become $x = 1$ and $x = -4$.
Attached the squared power to the wrong factor, giving the double zero at $x = 4$ and the single zero at $x = -1$.
Makes both slips at once: reverses the sign in each bracket and also squares the factor belonging to the single zero.

questions.solution_text:
A double zero at $x = -1$ corresponds to factor $(x + 1)^{2}$.
A single zero at $x = 4$ corresponds to factor $(x - 4)$.
$P(x) = (x + 1)^{2}(x - 4)$

questions.question_text: A monic polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $4$ has a double zero at $x = 2$, crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -3$ and $x = 0$. What is the value of $P(1)$?

options.why: Made a sign error when evaluating $(1 - 2)^{2} = 1$.
Multiplied $4 \times 4$ by squaring the $(x + 3)$ term incorrectly.
Assumed $P(1) = 0$ as if $1$ were also a zero of the polynomial.
